passage:
"Papa, you're as big as a giant!"
"Am I?" said Nilesh.
"A giant with a beard." Tarun, five, wrapped his arms around himself. "It's a bit chilly in here."
"Is it? I'm fine."
Tarun sniffed and said nothing. Nilesh looked at him. "Tarun, are you cold? Do you want a blanket?"
"Yes. Blanket, please."
"Next time you can just say, I want a blanket."

qa.q: What did Tarun say about the room?
qa.a: "It's a bit chilly in here."

qa.q: How might Tarun be feeling when he says it is chilly?
qa.a: He is probably cold and hopeful his father will fetch a blanket, since he hugs himself and later says yes to one. He might also have been just commenting on the room.

qa.q: How did Nilesh handle the hint?
qa.a: He asked directly whether Tarun was cold and taught him to say the request straight.

qa.q: How might Nilesh feel when he realises what the hint meant?
qa.a: A bit surprised that he missed it, but glad Tarun could say yes. 🙂

grounding: Shows a preschooler using a simile and a hint and an adult stating the request directly.

passage: Note from Lalremsiami, teacher. Shalini (5) told a friend at play, "Your bag is as big as a house!" They both giggled. At lunch she looked at the empty jug and said, "Wow, it's very dry here." I did not get it at first and asked, "Do you want water?" She nodded. I have decided to ask children directly when they hint, and to teach a full sentence: "Can I have water, please?"

qa.q: What did Shalini say about her friend's bag?
qa.a: That it was as big as a house.

qa.q: What was Shalini wanting when she said "it's very dry here"?
qa.a: Water. She hoped the teacher would guess, though she may have been just remarking on it.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami decide to do?
qa.a: Ask children directly when they hint, and teach a full sentence for requests.

qa.q: How might Shalini's friend see the bag remark?
qa.a: As a funny, friendly exaggeration, since they both giggled.

grounding: Shows a preschooler using a simile and an early hint that an adult misses, leading to teaching direct requests.

passage: On a cold evening in the village, Jasleen Nani sat on the charpai and said, “It's getting very dark in here.” She hoped Parul would switch on the bulb. Parul, drawing, said, “Yes, Nani, very dark,” and kept drawing. Nani smiled. “Parul, please switch on the light.” Parul jumped up and did. Then she looked at Nani, wrapped in her shawl. “Nani, you look as round as a laddoo!” Nani laughed so hard she coughed. “And you're as quick as a squirrel when I ask properly.”

qa.q: What did Parul say Nani looked as round as?
qa.a: A laddoo.

qa.q: What was Parul thinking when she said “Yes, Nani, very dark” and kept drawing?
qa.a: She was calm and absorbed in drawing and simply agreed with the fact, missing the hint that Nani wanted the light on.

qa.q: What did Nani learn works better with Parul?
qa.a: Stating the request directly, “please switch on the light,” instead of hinting.

qa.q: How did Nani feel about Parul's laddoo simile?
qa.a: She found it very funny and laughed so hard she coughed.

grounding: A preschooler misses her grandmother's hint but makes a playful simile, and a direct request works better.

passage: Rania came in from the market in Porto, arms full of bags. “Gabriel, my hands are very full,” she said, hoping he'd open the kitchen door. Gabriel looked up from his blocks. “Yes, you've got lots of bags.” He went back to building. Rania laughed and said, “Gabriel, please open the door for me.” He jumped up and held it wide. As she passed, he looked up at her. “Mama, you're as big as a giant with all those bags!” “A giant who says thank you,” she said.

qa.q: What did Rania hope Gabriel would open?
qa.a: The kitchen door.

qa.q: What was Gabriel thinking when he said “Yes, you've got lots of bags”?
qa.a: He was focused and content with his blocks and noticed the bags, but didn't understand that his mother was hinting for help.

qa.q: What worked better than hinting?
qa.a: Asking directly, “please open the door for me,” which Gabriel did at once.

qa.q: How might Rania feel about Gabriel's giant comment?
qa.a: She finds it funny and sweet, which is why she jokes back.

grounding: A preschooler misses his mother's hint but makes a playful simile, and a direct request works better.

passage: At the end of the nursery day, Anjali Ma'am looked at the floor and said, “Someone's shoes are in the middle of the room.” Nobody moved. Usha, whose shoes they were, nodded. “Yes, there are shoes.” Anjali smiled. “Usha, please put your shoes on the rack.” “Oh!” Usha picked them up and put them away. Then she said, “Ma'am, your bun is as big as a moon today.” Anjali laughed. “Thank you, I think. From now on I'll just say what I want.”

qa.q: Where did Anjali Ma'am ask Usha to put her shoes?
qa.a: On the rack.

qa.q: What does Usha's “Oh!” suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests she was surprised, suddenly understanding what was wanted; she had missed the hint and wasn't being difficult.

qa.q: What did Anjali Ma'am learn about hints with young children?
qa.a: That hints are often missed, so it is wiser to state requests directly, as she decides to do.

qa.q: How might the other children see Usha's moon comment?
qa.a: They might find it funny and try their own “as big as” comparisons.

grounding: A preschooler misses her teacher's hint but uses a playful simile, and the teacher resolves to state requests directly.

passage:
I'm Vinita, Uday's aunt. I was visiting on a cold evening. Uday stood next to his father and looked up. "Papa, you're as big as a giant!"

Later I said, "My, this floor is very messy," hoping Uday would put his blocks away. He kept building.

I tried, "Someone's blocks are everywhere." Nothing.

His father grinned at me and said, "Uday, please put the blocks in the box." Uday did it at once.

Then Uday pulled his knees up. "It's a bit chilly in here," he said, looking at the blanket on the sofa. His father laughed and tucked it round him.

qa.q: What did Uday say his father was as big as?
qa.a: A giant.

qa.q: What did Uday want when he said "It's a bit chilly in here"?
qa.a: He was most likely feeling cold and wanted the blanket, hinting while looking at it rather than asking directly. He may have felt shy about asking outright.

qa.q: What worked better than Vinita's hints about the blocks?
qa.a: A direct, clear request, "please put the blocks in the box," which Uday followed at once, because young children often miss hints.

qa.q: How does Uday's father see Uday's own hint about being chilly?
qa.a: He recognises it, laughs fondly, and tucks the blanket round him.

grounding: It shows a preschooler using a simple simile and a hint about the cold, while missing an adult's hints until the request is stated directly.
